pos: n. (hard and continued labor, especially such as fatigues body or mind)
etymology: From Old French toiler, to drag about, entangle, ultimately from Latin tudicula, a machine for crushing olives. The word carries in its root the picture of something wrung out under pressure, not merely worked at.
biblical_def:
Genesis names toil at both ends of a life. Lamech, naming his son Noah, looks forward to relief from it — this same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed — and the toil he means is the ground's own curse from Eden, the sweat of the brow that now attends every harvest. Joseph, decades later in Egypt, names his firstborn Manasseh, Forgetting, because God hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house — the toil there is not the ground's curse but the specific grief of the pit and Potiphar's house, the years a man spends before the LORD turns his captivity.

Between Lamech's hope and Joseph's relief sits the ordinary toil Ecclesiastes examines at length: what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? The Preacher's answer is not that toil is meaningless in itself but that toil pursued as its own reward, without reference to the God who gives the appetite to enjoy its fruit, dissolves into vexation. Christ's invitation stands against all three uses at once — Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest — not a promise that toil ends in this life, but that the curse's full weight need not be carried alone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): labor with pain and fatigue; hard work that exhausts the strength, either of body or mind.
webster_full: TOIL, n. Labor attended with fatigue and pain; hard work that wearies the body or mind.
LABOUR, n. Exertion of body or mind for the attainment of some object, especially when severe or continued.
CURSE, n. Malediction; a solemn or invocatory imprecation of evil; the sentence pronounced upon the ground for man's sin.
VEXATION, n. The act of vexing, or the state of being vexed; disquiet; agitation of mind; trouble.
REST, n. Cessation of labor or motion; repose; quiet; freedom from toil, disturbance, or pain.
scriptures: Gen 5:29
And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed.
And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house.
Ecc 2:22
For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun?
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: Toil is sold either as pure curse to be escaped or pure virtue to be maximized, when Scripture treats it as a real burden from the fall that God Himself proposes to carry with a man, not merely to end.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but it does face two opposite temptations, both older than any modern movement. One treats toil as an unmixed evil, something a righteous life should aim to escape as fully and as soon as possible. The other treats ceaseless toil itself as the mark of a well-lived life, as though the curse on the ground were actually a virtue to be pursued for its own sake.

Genesis will not allow either. The toil Lamech names is a real curse on a real ground, worth naming as a curse and worth hoping for relief from; the toil Joseph names is real grief God used and then, in His time, caused him to forget. Ecclesiastes' vexation is not toil as such but toil cut loose from the God who gives a man the ability to enjoy what his hands produce. Christ's rest is offered to the toiling and heavy laden precisely as toiling and heavy laden — not a call to stop working, but an invitation to stop carrying the curse's weight alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew itstsabown (H6093), toil, labor, sorrow; the word of the ground's curse in Genesis 3:17 and 5:29, and again of Joseph's own toil in Genesis 41:51.
roots_lines: Hebrew itstsabown (H6093) — toil, sorrow, labor; the very word pronounced over the ground in Genesis 3:17, echoed in 5:29 and 41:51.
Hebrew amal (H5999) — labor, toil, travail; the Preacher's own word for the vexation of Ecclesiastes 2:22.
Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to comfort, to console; the verb behind Noah's very name and Lamech's hope in Genesis 5:29.
Hebrew nashah (H5382, root of Manasseh) — to forget, to cause to forget; Joseph's own naming-word in Genesis 41:51.
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to grow weary with labor, to toil; the verb behind “labour” in Christ's invitation, Matthew 11:28.
usage: “this same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands” — Lamech's hope at Noah's birth.
“God hath made me forget all my toil” — Joseph's naming of Manasseh.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” — Christ's answer to toil itself.

pos: n. (the foremost part of anything; the face turned toward an approaching danger or an onlooker)
etymology: Latin frons, the forehead, the brow. The word arrives in English still carrying its bodily origin — a front is, at root, a face, the part of a thing that looks outward and takes the first blow or the first glance.
biblical_def:
Second Samuel places the word exactly where its Latin root would expect it: Joab, caught between the Syrians before him and the Ammonites behind, sees that the front of the battle was against him before and behind, and divides his army to meet both faces of the danger at once. It is the plainest military sense, the forward edge where the fighting is thickest, and Joab's tactical genius in that chapter is entirely a matter of correctly reading which front needs his best men.

Chronicles uses the same word of Solomon's temple porch, in the front of the house, the part first seen by anyone approaching — and the closely related frontlet, bound between the eyes at the LORD's own command in Exodus and Deuteronomy, puts the word on the body of every Israelite who kept the command literally. A frontlet sits exactly where a front faces outward: the forehead, the part of a man that meets every onlooker first. Scripture's uses of the word, taken together, describe the place where a hidden reality becomes visible to whoever is watching — a battle line's true danger, a temple's first impression, a covenant people's plainest confession, all located at the front, where nothing can any longer be concealed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the forepart of anything, as of an edifice or an army; the part that first presents itself to view.
webster_full: FRONT, n. The forehead; the foremost part or surface of a thing; the part that fronts or faces an observer.
ARRAY, n. Order; disposition in regular lines, as of troops prepared for battle.
PORCH, n. A portico; a covered walk, or a covered entrance to a building.
FRONTLET, n. A band worn on the forehead; something bound upon the front for a memorial.
TOKEN, n. A sign; a mark; something intended to represent or indicate another thing, or to serve as evidence of a fact.
scriptures: When Joab saw that the front of the battle was against him before and behind, he chose of all the choice men of Israel, and put them in array against the Syrians:

And the porch that was in the front of the house, the length of it was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the height was an hundred and twenty: and he overlaid it within with pure gold.
And it shall be for a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes: for by strength of hand the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt.
Deu 6:8
And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes.
corruption_summary: Front is used only of image and presentation, a face put on for others, when Scripture's own uses locate it as the place where a real danger or a real confession becomes visible, not a mask laid over one.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; front still names the forward or forepart of a thing. The principle worth recovering is that in every biblical use the front is where truth surfaces, not where it is managed. Joab's front is the actual place the actual danger will be met; the temple's front is the actual first stone laid; the frontlet is a physical, visible sign of a covenant a man has actually made in his heart.

The danger the word can be put to, though not one Scripture itself commits, is treating a front as a substitute for the substance behind it — a good front presented while nothing corresponding lies beneath. The frontlet commanded in Exodus and Deuteronomy resists exactly that temptation by design: it is meant to be the visible outworking of words already laid up in the heart, not a sign worn instead of that inward reality.
roots_summary: Hebrew panim (H6440), face, front, presence; the underlying idea behind frontlet and every Hebrew word for the forepart of a thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew paniym (H6440) — face, front, presence; the root sense behind “frontlets,” literally between the faces, the eyes.
Hebrew totaphah (H2903) — frontlets, bands; the specific noun of Exodus 13:16 and Deuteronomy 6:8.
Hebrew paniym milchamah — the face of the battle; the idiom behind “front of the battle” in 2 Samuel 10:9.
Hebrew ulam (H197) — a porch, a vestibule; the structure whose front Chronicles describes.
Hebrew owth (H226) — a sign, a token; the word paired with frontlets in both Exodus 13:16 and Deuteronomy 6:8.
usage: “the front of the battle was against him before and behind” — Joab's tactical reading at the walls of Rabbah.
“the porch that was in the front of the house” — the first sight of Solomon's temple.
“they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes” — the covenant word made visible on the body.

pos: a., n. (pertaining to a whole class or body, not particular; also, a chief officer commanding an army)
etymology: Latin generalis, from genus, kind, race, class — a thing that pertains to the whole kind rather than to one member of it. English kept both the adjective, of the whole, and the noun, the officer set over the whole army.
biblical_def:
Scripture uses the word in both its senses, and the two are worth holding side by side. In the ordinary military sense, Chronicles simply names the general of the king's army, Joab, an office of plain visible rank within the kingdom of Israel — a chief set over the whole of a specific, bounded force. It is the word Webster still gives first, and it is entirely unremarkable in its context.

Hebrews reaches for the same word to describe something no earthly general could ever command: believers who have come, in Christ, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven. The general assembly is not one local congregation among others but the whole company of the redeemed considered together, spirits of just men made perfect standing alongside the living, gathered at Mount Zion rather than at Sinai. The contrast the writer builds across the chapter is exact: Israel at Sinai could not bear even the general sound of the trumpet and the voice that spoke; believers in Christ have come to something greater still, a general assembly no army roster could number and no single general could ever command, because its head is God the Judge of all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): pertaining to a whole class, kind, or order; not special or particular; also, the chief commander of an army.
webster_full: GENERAL, a. Comprehending the whole, or a whole species; not special or particular; extending to the whole class.
GENERAL, n. A military officer who commands a whole army, or a large division of it.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together, in one place, usually for some common purpose.
FIRSTBORN, n. The first offspring; the eldest child; used figuratively of preeminence in rank or privilege.
PARTICULAR, a. Pertaining to a single person or thing; individual; distinct from others; not general.
scriptures: And after Ahithophel was Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar: and the general of the king's army was Joab.
But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels,
To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: General is treated as a synonym for vague or unspecific, when Hebrews uses it of the single most definite gathering in all Scripture — every redeemed spirit, named in heaven, under one Judge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; general still names the whole class as against the particular member. The principle worth recovering is that Hebrews' general assembly is not a fuzzy or approximate gathering — it is comprehensive in exactly the sense a Roman census or a military muster roll is comprehensive, taking in every one of a defined class without remainder.

The writer's whole argument in Hebrews twelve depends on this precision. Israel at Sinai met a general terror they could not bear to hear generally described, let alone endure specifically. Believers in Christ have come to a general assembly that is, if anything, more exactly accounted than Sinai's trembling crowd — every name written in heaven, every spirit of a just man made perfect, gathered under one Judge who misses none of them. The word's comprehensiveness is precisely the ground of its comfort.
roots_summary: Greek panegyris (G3831), a general or festal assembly, a whole gathered company; the specific noun behind Hebrews 12:23.
roots_lines: Greek panegyris (G3831) — a general assembly, a festal gathering of a whole people; the word translated “general assembly” in Hebrews 12:23.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — a called-out assembly, a church; the second noun of the same verse, of the firstborn.
Greek prototokos (G4416) — firstborn; the title given the whole company, sharing Christ's own preeminence.
Greek kriths (G2923) — a judge; the title given God over the whole assembly named in this verse.
Hebrew sar tsaba — a captain or general of the host; the ordinary Old Testament military title behind Joab's own office.
usage: “the general of the king's army was Joab” — the plain military office in Chronicles.
“the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven” — the whole company of the redeemed in Hebrews.
“to God the Judge of all” — the one head over that entire general assembly.

pos: a. (relating to a single person or thing, as distinguished from others; individual; specific)
etymology: Latin particula, a small part, diminutive of pars, a part. What is particular is, at root, a matter reduced to its individual pieces rather than considered as a whole.
biblical_def:
Acts uses the word of Paul's own report to James and the elders at Jerusalem: called to account for a ministry many had heard rumors of, Paul does not summarize in general terms but declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry — item by item, case by case, so that the elders could weigh the specific facts rather than the general reputation. Particularity here is a form of honesty; a man willing to be specific is a man willing to be checked.

Paul's other use of the word, to the Corinthians, applies the same precision to the body of Christ itself: Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. The doctrine of the body only holds together because both halves are equally true — the church is one body, and every believer in it is a distinct, particular, individually named member of it, with a particular gift and a particular function that no other member can supply in his place. A theology of the church that only ever speaks generally, never particularly, has lost exactly the thing Paul insists on in the same breath he insists on the body's unity: the whole is real, and so, without contradiction, is every particular part of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): relating to a single person or thing; individual; distinct from others; not general; specific.
webster_full: PARTICULAR, a. Individual; distinct from others; noting a single thing or person, as opposed to general or universal.
MEMBER, n. A part of an animal body, as an arm, leg, or organ; figuratively, an individual of a body or society.
DECLARE, v.t. To make clear or manifest; to make known explicitly; to publish, or proclaim distinctly.
MINISTRY, n. The office, duties, or functions of a minister, particularly one appointed to teach and administer the gospel.
BODY, n. A collective mass; a number of individuals or particulars united or considered as one whole.
scriptures: And when he had saluted them, he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry.
And when they heard it, they glorified the Lord, and said unto him, Thou seest, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are which believe; and they are all zealous of the law:
Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular.
For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ.
corruption_summary: Particular is treated as the opposite of significant, the merely local detail set against the important general picture, when Acts uses it precisely to mean the kind of accountable specificity that lets a claim actually be tested.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; particular still names the individual instance rather than the general class. The principle worth recovering is Paul's own use of it before the Jerusalem elders: a man with nothing to hide is a man willing to be particular, to name the actual cases rather than rest on a general and unfalsifiable claim to have done a great work.

First Corinthians applies the same precision to church life, and refuses to let the doctrine of one body dissolve any believer's particular identity into an undifferentiated mass. Every member is named in particular, with a particular gift, in the very passage that most insists on the unity of the whole. A church that speaks only in generalities about the body of Christ, never in particulars about its actual members and their actual gifts, has not honored the doctrine Paul is teaching — it has quietly dropped half of it.
roots_summary: Greek kata heis hekastos (G1520/G1538), one by one, each severally; the phrase behind “in particular” in 1 Corinthians 12:27.
roots_lines: Greek kata heis (G2596/G1520) — according to one, one by one; the idiom behind “in particular” in 1 Corinthians 12:27.
Greek melos (G3196) — a member, a limb; the noun naming each particular part of the one body.
Greek kathexes (G2517) — in order, one after another; the manner Paul elsewhere reports things (Luke 1:3), close kin to the particularity of Acts 21:19.
Greek diegeomai (G1334) — to relate fully, to declare in detail; the sense behind “declared particularly.”
Greek ethnos (G1484) — a nation, a Gentile; the object of the particular things God had wrought through Paul's ministry.
usage: “he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles” — Paul's accountable report at Jerusalem.
“ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular” — the individual standing of every believer within the one body.
“the body is one, and hath many members” — the unity that particularity never dissolves.

pos: a. (particular; distinguished from others of the same kind; set apart for a peculiar purpose)
etymology: Latin specialis, from species, a kind or sort, itself from specere, to look at or behold. What is special has been looked at and singled out from among its kind, not merely noticed but set apart.
biblical_def:
Deuteronomy's use of the word names the whole basis of Israel's election: the LORD thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth. The choosing precedes and grounds the specialness; Israel is not special because of some quality found in her and then rewarded, but special because the LORD set His love upon her and chose her, a truth Deuteronomy states plainly a few verses earlier — not for her number, for she was the fewest of all people, but for His own love and oath to the fathers.

Peter's letter to scattered believers takes the same word, transposed now into the new covenant, and applies it without qualification to the church: ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people — the same idea of a people specially marked out, purchased now not by descent from Abraham but by the blood of Christ. The special standing Israel had did not, in the end, belong to national descent as such; it always pointed forward to a special people gathered from every nation who would shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. What makes either people special was never anything special found in them first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): particular; peculiar; distinguished from others by some circumstance; designed for a particular purpose.
webster_full: SPECIAL, a. Particular; distinguished from what is general or ordinary; designed for a specific object or occasion.
PECULIAR, a. Belonging exclusively to one person or thing; particular; not common to others.
CHOSEN, a. Selected from a number, by preference; elected; taken in preference to others.
PRIESTHOOD, n. The office and character of a priest; the priestly order collectively considered.
MARVELLOUS, a. Exciting wonder or surprise; astonishing; strange beyond credibility, yet true.
scriptures: Deu 7:6
For thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God: the LORD thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth.
Deu 7:7
The LORD did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest of all people:
Deu 7:8

But because the LORD loved you, and because he would keep the oath which he had sworn unto your fathers, hath the LORD brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondmen, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
corruption_summary: Special is used to flatter a felt uniqueness earned by talent or performance, when Deuteronomy and Peter both ground it entirely in a love and a choice that had nothing to do with the recipient's own merit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word, but the biblical doctrine behind it runs directly against a very old and very persistent instinct — the assumption that being called special must mean being especially deserving. Deuteronomy removes that assumption at the root: Israel was the fewest of all peoples, chosen for the LORD's own love and oath, not for anything special found in her first.

First Peter transfers the identical logic to the church without softening it — a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people, called out of darkness by a light none of them supplied for themselves. The special status either people held was never a verdict on their own worth; it was, and remains, a verdict on the God who set His love upon them, which is exactly why the purpose named in the same verse is not self-congratulation but praise directed entirely away from the special people and onto the one who called them.
roots_summary: Hebrew segullah (H5459), a peculiar treasure, a special possession; the covenant word behind both “special people” in Deuteronomy and “peculiar people” in 1 Peter.
roots_lines: Hebrew segullah (H5459) — a peculiar treasure, a special possession; the word behind “special people” in Deuteronomy 7:6, also used at Exodus 19:5.
Hebrew bachar (H977) — to choose, to select; the covenant verb of election in Deuteronomy 7:6-7.
Hebrew chashaq (H2836) — to set love upon, to delight in; the ground of the choosing named in Deuteronomy 7:7-8.
Greek laos eis peripoiesin (G2992/G4047) — a people for a possession; the Greek behind “peculiar people” in 1 Peter 2:9, the same idea as segullah.
Greek genos eklekton (G1085/G1588) — a chosen generation, a chosen race; Peter's own opening phrase in the same verse.
usage: “the LORD thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself” — Israel's election in Deuteronomy.
“because the LORD loved you” — the ground of that special standing, not Israel's own merit.
“a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people” — the same standing transferred to the church.

pos: a. (one only; not double or divided; free from duplicity; sincere and whole in intention)
etymology: Latin singulus, one at a time, one by one. English kept both the count — a single thing, not two — and the moral sense that grew from it, a single eye or a single heart being one undivided in its aim rather than split between two.
biblical_def:
Christ's teaching on the eye, given in nearly identical words in Matthew and Luke, turns entirely on this second, moral sense of the word: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. The eye here stands for the whole inward aim of a man — what he is actually looking at, actually seeking, actually serving. A single eye is one fixed on one object without division; and Matthew's verse, read in its context between treasure laid up in heaven and the flat statement that no man can serve two masters, makes plain what the one object is meant to be.

The alternative Christ names is not merely distraction but an eye that is evil, and the whole body correspondingly full of darkness — the darkness of a man trying to serve God and mammon at once, whose inward light, precisely because it is divided, becomes no light at all. Singleness of eye, in this teaching, is not a a call to simplicity for its own sake; it is the necessary condition for a man's whole inward life to be illuminated by anything, because a light split between two objects has, by definition, stopped being a single light and become a confusion of shadows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one only, not double; also, sincere; unmixed with deceit or hypocrisy; free from duplicity of intention.
webster_full: SINGLE, a. One only; not double; also, sincere, honest, free from artifice or duplicity of aim.
EYE, n. The organ of sight; figuratively, the mind's power of perceiving, attending, and desiring.
LIGHT, n. That which makes objects visible; figuratively, knowledge, understanding, or spiritual illumination.
DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; figuratively, ignorance, sin, or spiritual blindness.
MAMMON, n. Riches; wealth personified as an object of worship rivaling the true God.
scriptures: Mat 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Mat 6:23
But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness.
corruption_summary: Single-mindedness is praised as a mere personality trait, useful for productivity, when Christ ties it directly to the impossibility of serving two masters and warns that a divided eye fills the whole body with darkness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself; single still means one and undivided. The principle worth recovering is the exact placement of Christ's saying, sandwiched between the command to lay up treasure in heaven rather than on earth and the flat statement that no man can serve two masters. The single eye is not a technique for a better life; it is the visible symptom of an undivided allegiance.

The warning cuts against every attempt to keep two ultimate loyalties running side by side, God and mammon, treasure on earth and treasure in heaven, hoping the eye can somehow serve both without going dark. Christ's language allows for no such balance: an eye that is not single is called evil, not merely inefficient, and the darkness it produces is total, filling the whole body, precisely because the light a man has was never meant to be divided in the first place.
roots_summary: Greek haplous (G573), single, simple, without folds; the word behind Christ's teaching on the eye in Matthew 6:22 and Luke 11:34.
roots_lines: Greek haplous (G573) — single, simple, sound, without folds or doubling; the adjective behind “single” in both Gospel accounts.
Greek haplotes (G572) — singleness, simplicity, sincerity; the noun form used elsewhere of a single-hearted generosity (2 Corinthians 8:2, Romans 12:8).
Greek poneros (G4190) — evil, bad, of poor quality; the word behind “evil” describing the divided eye.
Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness; the total condition of a body whose light has become divided.
Aramaic mamona (G3126) — mammon, riches personified; the second master a single eye cannot also serve.
usage: “if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” — the promise of undivided sight.
“if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness” — the warning that frames it.
“Ye cannot serve God and mammon” — the divided allegiance a single eye refuses.

pos: v.t., n. (to bind or fasten with a cord or band; that which fastens or unites)
etymology: Saxon tigan, to bind. A tie is the plainest possible fastening — a knot, a cord, a bond drawn tight enough to hold two things, or two parties, together.
biblical_def:
The word appears in the Authorized Version in scenes of the most ordinary, practical binding: the blue lace tied to fasten the high priest's plate high upon the mitre in Exodus, and the milch kine the Philistines are told to tie to a new cart, untrained animals bound to a task no ox had ever been made to pull alone, so that their unnatural, untaught obedience in going straight toward Bethshemesh would prove whose hand had really sent the plague upon them. Both ties are literal cords doing literal work, and in both cases the tying is not incidental to the story but the very mechanism by which something is revealed — the plate stays where the LORD commanded, and the kine go where no hand drove them.

The kine bound to the cart make the clearest case. Their calves are shut up at home, every natural instinct pulling them backward, and yet, tied to a cart they have never pulled, they go straight up the highway lowing as they go, turning neither to the right hand nor to the left. A tie meant only to hold two boards of a cart together becomes, in that chapter, the means by which even the Philistines are forced to conclude their own affliction had come from the God of Israel and no other. What is tied together, in Scripture's own use of the word, is rarely only the thing named — a plate to a mitre, an animal to a cart — but very often the visible sign and an invisible testimony bound fast to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to bind, as with a cord, band, or string; to fasten; to unite, or hold together, by any bond.
webster_full: TIE, v.t. To bind with a cord, string or ligament; to fasten, or to knot together, for security.
FASTEN, v.t. To fix firmly; to make fast; to attach one thing to another so it cannot easily be separated.
LACE, n. A string or cord used for fastening, as of a garment or an ornament.
YOKE, n. A frame of wood by which two draft animals are joined at the neck for working together.
CART, n. A carriage with two wheels, drawn by beasts of burden, for conveying loads.
scriptures: And they tied unto it a lace of blue, to fasten it on high upon the mitre; as the LORD commanded Moses.
Now therefore make a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke, and tie the kine to the cart, and bring their calves home from them:

And the kine took the straight way to the way of Bethshemesh, and went along the highway, lowing as they went, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left; and the lords of the Philistines went after them unto the border of Bethshemesh.
And thou shalt put it on a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre; upon the forefront of the mitre it shall be.
corruption_summary: A tie is treated as sentimental or arbitrary, a mere attachment of feeling, when Scripture's uses show a tie doing real, observable, evidentiary work — holding a priestly plate in place, proving a plague's true source.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a tie still fastens two things together. The principle worth recovering is how much weight Scripture is willing to hang on so small a mechanism. The blue lace tying the plate to the mitre is a minor detail of priestly dress that the text nonetheless records with the same formula given the LORD's whole tabernacle pattern — as the LORD commanded Moses.

The tied kine of 1 Samuel 6 carry the greater weight still. Untrained animals, tied to a cart, with every natural pull toward home, instead go the one direction no natural instinct would send them — and the Philistine lords, watching, are left with no explanation but the one the text has already given. A tie meant only to hold an animal to a cart becomes, by the plainest of means, the proof the LORD needed no miracle beyond ordinary rope and an extraordinary refusal of ordinary instinct.
roots_summary: Hebrew acar (H631), to tie, to bind, to harness; the verb behind both the priestly lace of Exodus and the yoked kine of 1 Samuel.
roots_lines: Hebrew acar (H631) — to tie, bind, harness; used of binding an animal to a task, the verb behind 1 Samuel 6:7, 10.
Hebrew pathiyl (H6616) — a cord, a thread, a lace; the word behind the blue lace of Exodus 28:37 and 39:31.
Hebrew ol (H5923) — a yoke; explicitly excluded from these kine, on which there hath come no yoke, so the miracle could not be credited to training.
Hebrew garah (H1641) — to low, to bellow; the sound the kine made even as they went the one direction against their nature.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — a way, a road; the straight way the tied kine kept without turning, right hand or left.
usage: “they tied unto it a lace of blue, to fasten it on high upon the mitre” — the priestly plate secured exactly as commanded.
“tie the kine to the cart, and bring their calves home from them” — the test the Philistine priests devised.
“the kine took the straight way... and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left” — the tie that became the proof.

pos: v.i., n. (to speak softly, with suppressed voice; a low, secret utterance, often carrying suspicion or slander)
etymology: Saxon hwisprian, imitative of the sound itself — a soft, breathy hiss of speech. English kept the word close to its sound from the beginning, and Scripture's uses lean almost entirely toward the darker use a lowered voice makes possible.
biblical_def:
David's own court supplies the clearest example of the word's ordinary meaning in Scripture. As his child by Bathsheba lies dying, his servants dare not tell him plainly what has happened; instead they whispered, and David, watching them murmur among themselves rather than speak to him directly, correctly reads the whispering itself as the message — David perceived that the child was dead. The whisper here is not malicious, only fearful, but it shows the word's essential shape: information passed in a lowered voice, meant to be understood by its manner as much as its content.

The Psalms turn the same word toward genuine malice. David, elsewhere surrounded by enemies, laments that all that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt — the low voice now doing the specific work of conspiracy, plotting harm precisely where it cannot be overheard or answered. Romans lists whisperers among the marks of a mind given over to a reprobate condition, in company with backbiters and haters of God, because a whisper of this kind is slander wearing the disguise of discretion: it claims the appearance of private caution while doing the actual work of public harm, exactly the opposite of the open rebuke Scripture commands between brothers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to speak with a low, hissing voice; to utter words softly and privately; often, to speak secretly against another.
webster_full: WHISPER, v.i. To speak with a low voice, or under the breath; to utter words with a soft, hissing sound.
MURMUR, v.i. To make a low, continued sound; to complain in a low, muttering voice.
BACKBITER, n. One who slanders, censures, or speaks evil of another in his absence.
DEVISE, v.t. To contrive; to plan; to invent, especially with evil intent.
REBUKE, v.t. To reprove openly and directly; to chide for a fault to a person's face.
scriptures: But when David saw that his servants whispered, David perceived that the child was dead: therefore David said unto his servants, Is the child dead? And they said, He is dead.
Psa 41:7
All that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt.
Rom 1:29
Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,
Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.
corruption_summary: Whispering is treated as harmless discretion, softer and therefore kinder than open speech, when Scripture repeatedly ties the whisper specifically to conspiracy and slander done precisely where it cannot be challenged.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; a whisper is still a lowered, secretive voice. The principle worth recovering is Leviticus's own alternative to it, given in the same command that forbids hating a brother in the heart: open rebuke to a neighbour's face, spoken so it can be answered, rather than a lowered voice spoken so it cannot.

David's own servants whisper out of fear rather than malice, and Scripture does not condemn them for it; the sharper warning falls on the whisperers of Psalm 41 and Romans 1, who use the lowered voice precisely because they intend harm that daylight speech would expose to correction. The whisper's danger is not its volume but its purpose — it is speech deliberately arranged to do its damage before the one spoken against can hear it, weigh it, or answer it.
roots_summary: Hebrew lachash (H3907), to whisper, to charm; Greek psithuristes (G5588), a whisperer, listed among the marks of a reprobate mind in Romans 1:29.
roots_lines: Hebrew lachash (H3907) — to whisper, to charm by a low voice; the same root gives the word for a serpent's charmer.
Hebrew rakal (H7270) — to go about as a talebearer; the underlying activity behind the whispering Psalm 41 condemns.
Greek psithuristes (G5588) — a whisperer, a secret slanderer; the noun in Romans 1:29's catalog of a reprobate mind.
Greek katalalos (G2637) — a backbiter, a speaker-against; listed beside whisperers in the same verse.
Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, to rebuke, to decide; the open alternative Leviticus 19:17 commands in place of the hidden whisper.
usage: “when David saw that his servants whispered, David perceived that the child was dead” — a fearful, not malicious, whisper.
“all that hate me whisper together against me” — the malicious whisper of conspiracy.
“thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour” — the open speech Scripture commands instead.

pos: n. (the edible seeds of leguminous plants, as beans, lentiles, and peas; plain food, as opposed to rich fare)
etymology: Latin puls, a thick porridge or pottage, the staple grain-mash of the Roman poor. The word narrowed in English to the seeds themselves — beans, lentiles, peas — the plainest and least esteemed of ordinary food.
biblical_def:
Daniel's test before the prince of the eunuchs is built entirely around this one humble word. Having purposed in his heart not to defile himself with the king's meat or wine, Daniel proposes an alternative so modest it barely counts as a request: Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink. He does not ask for a theological exemption or a public confrontation; he asks for beans and water for ten days, and offers to let the results speak for themselves.

The result is the whole point of the chapter: at the end of ten days, the four young men fed on pulse alone appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's rich portion, and Melzar took away the king's meat and continued giving them pulse. Second Samuel uses the same word in an entirely different scene — parched pulse among the provisions brought to David's exhausted army in the wilderness, plain food doing plain, sustaining work for men in flight. Between the two scenes, pulse becomes an unlikely emblem of a single principle: that faithfulness in a small, unglamorous matter, kept without fanfare, can carry a strength that no rich table ever supplied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the edible seeds of leguminous plants, as pease, beans, and lentiles; food of a plain and simple kind.
webster_full: PULSE, n. Leguminous plants, or their seeds, as beans, pease, and lentiles, used for food.
PORTION, n. A part or share allotted or distributed; especially, a share of food assigned to a person.
DEFILE, v.t. To make unclean or impure; to corrupt; to render ceremonially unfit.
PROVE, v.t. To try; to test by experiment or experience; to establish the truth of by trial.
FAIR, a. Beautiful; pleasing to the eye; also, of a healthy or well-favored appearance.
scriptures: Dan 1:8

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
Dan 1:12
Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.
Dan 1:16
Thus Melzar took away the portion of their meat, and the wine that they should drink; and gave them pulse.
Brought beds, and basons, and earthen vessels, and wheat, and barley, and flour, and parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse,
corruption_summary: Plain, unglamorous obedience is treated as spiritually unimpressive next to visible sacrifice or public confrontation, when Daniel's whole test is built on beans and water quietly outperforming the king's own table.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; pulse still names the humblest grade of food. The principle worth recovering is how deliberately small Daniel's actual act of faithfulness was. He does not demand a public exemption from Babylon's whole court, does not stage a confrontation with Nebuchadnezzar, does not ask for anything except ten days and beans — and lets the outcome, not the gesture, do the persuading.

The chapter's verdict is unambiguous: the pulse-fed young men were fairer and fatter than the whole company fed on the king's portion, and their plain diet becomes the quiet, undeniable evidence behind everything Daniel accomplishes in the rest of the book. Faithfulness in the smallest and least impressive matter, kept without fanfare and proven rather than merely asserted, is exactly the pattern pulse is made to carry in this text.
roots_summary: Hebrew zeroa (H2235), seed, sown food; the general word behind the pulse Daniel requests, related to the Hebrew for sowing seed.
roots_lines: Hebrew zeroa (H2235) — that which is sown, seed, vegetable food; the word rendered “pulse” in Daniel 1:12, 16.
Hebrew ga'al (H1351) — to defile, to pollute; the verb behind Daniel's purpose not to defile himself with the king's meat.
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to try, to test, to prove; the verb behind Daniel's own request, Prove thy servants.
Hebrew bariy (H1277) — fat, well-fed, fleshy; the word describing the pulse-fed youths' appearance in Daniel 1:15.
Hebrew qaliy (H7039) — parched, roasted grain; the preparation named of the pulse brought to David's army in 2 Samuel 17:28.
usage: “let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink” — Daniel's modest, testable request.
“Melzar took away the portion of their meat... and gave them pulse” — the outcome that vindicated it.
“parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse” — the same plain food sustaining David's army.

pos: n. (the meaning of words rightly understood; also, the faculty of perceiving and judging by experience)
etymology: Latin sensus, from sentire, to feel or perceive. The word carries both the bodily faculty of feeling and, by extension, the mind's grasp of a meaning — what a passage or a matter actually amounts to once rightly perceived.
biblical_def:
Nehemiah's account of the great public reading of the law, after the exile, describes exactly what right teaching is meant to accomplish: the Levites read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Three things happen in that single verse and none of them is optional — the text is read clearly, its sense is given, and the hearers actually come to understand. A congregation could hear every word of the law read aloud and still miss its sense entirely without the second step; Ezra's Levites are recorded doing all three because Scripture treats the giving of sense as real teaching work, not an afterthought to public reading.

Hebrews uses the word of a different, slower kind of understanding, formed not by one clear exposition but by long practice: mature believers are those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil, in contrast to those still needing milk. Paul's warning to Corinth about the natural man who cannot receive spiritual things, because they are spiritually discerned, sits behind both passages as their deepest ground: sense, in the fullest biblical meaning, is never mere intellectual comprehension of words on a page, but a trained capacity, given by the Spirit and sharpened by use, to perceive what a text or a situation actually is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): perception by the intellect; the meaning of a word, sentence, or discourse; also, the faculty of feeling or perceiving.
webster_full: SENSE, n. Perception by the mind; the meaning of words or passages when rightly understood; also, one of the bodily faculties of feeling.
DISTINCTLY, adv. Clearly; plainly; so as to be perceived or understood without confusion.
DISCERN, v.t. To perceive by the eye or the understanding; to distinguish one thing from another with judgment.
EXERCISE, v.t. To train by practice; to develop or strengthen a faculty by repeated use.
NATURAL, a. Pertaining to nature; not spiritual or regenerate; belonging to man's condition apart from grace.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Pro 2:3
Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding;
corruption_summary: Sense is reduced to raw feeling or private impression, whatever a passage seems to mean to the individual reader, when Nehemiah's Levites give the sense publicly and accountably, and Hebrews ties true discernment to disciplined practice, not private intuition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, but it does face a real drift in how the sense of a text is thought to be obtained. Nehemiah's account is careful to show the sense of the law arrived at through a public, accountable process — distinct reading, active exposition, and confirmed understanding — not a feeling any hearer was left to generate privately from the words alone.

Hebrews adds the discipline of time to the same picture: senses exercised to discern good and evil are the product of sustained use, not a single moment of insight, still less an emotional impression mistaken for understanding. Paul's word to Corinth explains why sense of this depth cannot be manufactured by cleverness alone — the natural man, however intelligent, cannot receive what is spiritually discerned, because the sense Scripture means here is finally a gift of the Spirit exercised through faithful practice, not a private feeling summoned at will.
roots_summary: Hebrew sekel (H7922), understanding, insight; Greek aisthesis (G144) and aistheterion (G5124), the faculties of perception behind “senses” in Hebrews 5:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew sekel (H7922) — understanding, insight, discretion; the underlying idea behind “gave the sense” in Nehemiah 8:8.
Hebrew biyn (H995) — to discern, to understand; the verb behind “caused them to understand the reading” in the same verse.
Greek aistheterion (G5124) — a faculty of perception, an organ of sense; the noun behind “senses” in Hebrews 5:14.
Greek diakrisis (G1253) — discernment, a distinguishing; the compound idea behind “to discern both good and evil.”
Greek psuchikos (G5591) — natural, unspiritual, of the soul only; the word behind “natural man” in 1 Corinthians 2:14.
usage: “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” — public, accountable teaching in Nehemiah.
“have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil” — discernment formed by sustained practice in Hebrews.
“the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God” — the limit no cleverness alone can cross.
